stem: Primary Eye Care (PEC) is best described as which of the following?
options: The integration of essential eye health services into the general primary health care (PHC) system
A specialist tertiary service available only in teaching hospitals
A private insurance product covering only spectacles
A research programme with no direct patient-care component

stem: Primary Eye Care is usually delivered by which category of health workers, with a functional referral pathway to secondary and tertiary eye units?
options: Non-specialist health workers such as community health officers, PHC nurses, and community health extension workers (CHEWs)
Consultant ophthalmologists exclusively
Pharmaceutical sales representatives exclusively
Hospital administrators exclusively

stem: The WHO African Region package of primary eye care interventions is built around health promotion, basic treatment, prompt referral, and which other core component?
options: Screening/early detection
Advanced laser surgery performed by lay community volunteers
Exclusive distribution of free spectacles with no other service
Tertiary-level organ transplantation

stem: In Nigeria, the concept of Primary Eye Care underlies the National Eye Health Policy and which global programme?
options: VISION 2020: The Right to Sight
The National Malaria Elimination Programme
The Expanded Programme on Immunization exclusively
The National Blood Transfusion Policy

stem: Refractive errors such as myopia, hypermetropia, astigmatism, and presbyopia are considered the single commonest cause of visual impairment worldwide, yet remain widely uncorrected in low-resource settings for which reason?
options: Poor access to refraction and optical services
Universal, complete access to free spectacles in every community
A complete absence of any demand for corrective lenses
Refractive error being untreatable with existing technology

stem: Repeated trachoma infection scars the eyelid and causes the eyelashes to turn inward, a condition known as which of the following?
options: Trichiasis
Leukocoria
Xerophthalmia
Phacomorphic glaucoma

stem: Onchocerciasis (river blindness) is transmitted by which vector, which breeds in fast-flowing rivers?
options: The blackfly (Simulium)
The mosquito (Anopheles)
The housefly (Musca domestica)
The tsetse fly

stem: Vitamin A deficiency can progress to keratomalacia, which refers to which process?
options: Corneal melting
Thickening of the eyelid margin
Clouding of the lens
Retinal detachment

stem: Retinopathy of prematurity, a congenital/genetic cause of blindness, is specifically associated with which exposure in preterm or low-birth-weight babies?
options: Uncontrolled oxygen therapy
Excessive maternal vitamin A supplementation during the third trimester
Routine antibiotic eye prophylaxis at birth
Breastfeeding exclusively for the first six months

stem: Retinoblastoma in children presents classically with which finding?
options: A white pupillary reflex, described as leukocoria or 'cat's eye reflex'
A wing-shaped growth extending onto the cornea
A red, painful eye with purulent discharge
Complete absence of the globe at birth

stem: In the Nigerian context, cataract is described as the single leading cause of blindness, with a large backlog of untreated cases due to which combination of factors?
options: Poor awareness, cost, distance to surgical services, and fear of surgery
Universal free access to surgery with no remaining backlog
An oversupply of surgeons relative to patients needing care
A complete absence of any surgical option nationwide

stem: Glaucoma, the second leading cause of blindness in Nigeria, is sometimes called 'the silent thief of sight' because it is often which of the following?
options: Asymptomatic until advanced
Always accompanied by severe pain from the very first symptom
Exclusively a disease of childhood
Always visible to an observer as a white pupil

stem: According to the WHO classification of visual impairment based on presenting visual acuity in the better eye, blindness is defined as visual acuity less than 3/60, OR which alternative criterion?
options: A visual field of less than 10 degrees around central fixation
A visual field of more than 90 degrees around central fixation
Any visual acuity below 6/6
Complete inability to perceive color

stem: 'Low vision' is commonly used to describe which category of visual impairment?
options: Moderate to severe visual impairment, worse than 6/18 but better than the blindness threshold, even with best correction
Total and complete loss of all light perception
Visual acuity of exactly 6/6 in both eyes
A visual field defect affecting only peripheral vision with normal central acuity

stem: 'Avoidable blindness' is best described as the sum of which two categories?
options: Preventable blindness and curable/treatable blindness
Congenital blindness and acquired blindness
Unilateral blindness and bilateral blindness
Moderate visual impairment and severe visual impairment

stem: According to the Nigeria National Blindness and Visual Impairment Survey (2005-2007), what was the estimated prevalence of blindness among adults aged 40 years and above?
options: 4.2%, translating to an estimated 1.13 million blind adults
0.2%, translating to fewer than 50,000 blind adults
25%, translating to over 10 million blind adults
42%, affecting nearly half the adult population

stem: Blindness prevalence in Nigeria was found to be highest in which geopolitical zone, which also carries the largest share of the country's blind population?
options: The North-West geopolitical zone
The South-West geopolitical zone only
The South-South geopolitical zone only
The Federal Capital Territory exclusively

stem: Approximately what percentage of blindness in Nigeria is avoidable, that is, preventable or treatable, according to the national survey?
options: Approximately 84%
Approximately 8%
Approximately 50%
Approximately 100%, with no exceptions whatsoever

stem: According to the national survey data cited, approximately what percentage of blindness in Nigeria is attributed to cataract, making it the single leading cause?
options: Approximately 43%
Approximately 4.3%
Approximately 93%
Approximately 16.7%

stem: Which of the following is explicitly listed as a risk factor contributing to the causes of blindness in Nigeria, related to household wealth?
options: Poverty, since cataract surgical coverage and spectacle wear are both lowest among the poor
High household income exceeding national averages
Urban residence with easy access to tertiary eye hospitals
Advanced postgraduate education in ophthalmology

stem: Which of the following is listed as a leading cause specifically of CHILDHOOD blindness in Nigeria, alongside congenital cataract and congenital glaucoma?
options: Corneal scarring from vitamin A deficiency and measles
Age-related macular degeneration
Diabetic retinopathy from long-standing adult-onset diabetes
Primary open-angle glaucoma of late adulthood

stem: Which level of prevention is aimed at preventing an eye problem from occurring at all?
options: Primary prevention
Secondary prevention
Tertiary prevention
Quaternary prevention

stem: Health education on eye hygiene, such as 'face-washing' to reduce trachoma transmission, falls under which level of prevention?
options: Primary prevention
Secondary prevention
Tertiary prevention
None of these levels, as hygiene education is unrelated to prevention

stem: Instillation of prophylactic eye drops or ointment, such as tetracycline, into every newborn's eyes immediately after delivery is a primary prevention measure aimed at preventing which condition?
options: Ophthalmia neonatorum
Retinoblastoma
Pterygium
Age-related macular degeneration

stem: Which primary prevention measure specifically targets onchocerciasis through vector and parasite control?
options: Community-directed treatment with ivermectin (CDTI) and environmental control of blackfly breeding sites
Routine cataract surgery outreach camps
Genetic counselling for inherited retinal dystrophies
Provision of low-vision magnifying devices

stem: Which level of prevention involves early detection and prompt treatment to limit progression or complications of an eye condition?
options: Secondary prevention
Primary prevention
Tertiary prevention
There is no such level described in the material

stem: Intraocular pressure checks for adults over 40 or those with a family history of glaucoma, and regular fundus examination for diabetics and hypertensives, are examples of which level of prevention?
options: Secondary prevention, through screening of high-risk groups
Primary prevention, through health education alone
Tertiary prevention, through surgical intervention alone
A level of prevention not addressed anywhere in the material

stem: Training primary health workers and community volunteers to recognise 'red flag' eye conditions requiring urgent referral is an example of which level of prevention?
options: Secondary prevention
Primary prevention exclusively
Tertiary prevention exclusively
A purely administrative task unrelated to any level of prevention

stem: Which of the following is specifically listed as a 'red flag' eye condition requiring urgent referral?
options: A white pupil in a child
Mild, chronic dry eye with no other symptoms
A fully corrected refractive error with normal vision
A healed, non-infected corneal scar with stable vision

stem: Case-finding and referral of cataract patients for surgery BEFORE complications such as phacomorphic glaucoma develop is an example of which level of prevention?
options: Secondary prevention
Primary prevention
A form of tertiary prevention exclusively, with no secondary component
Not a recognised prevention activity at all

stem: Which level of prevention involves treatment and rehabilitation to limit disability once eye damage has already occurred?
options: Tertiary prevention
Primary prevention
Secondary prevention
There is no tertiary level described in the material

stem: Cataract surgery, including outreach and free surgical camps to reach the rural poor, is an example of which level of prevention?
options: Tertiary prevention
Primary prevention exclusively
Secondary prevention exclusively
A level of prevention not mentioned in the material

stem: Provision of low-vision services, such as magnifying devices and optical aids, for those with irreversible visual impairment falls under which level of prevention?
options: Tertiary prevention
Primary prevention
Secondary prevention
None of these levels

stem: VISION 2020: The Right to Sight is a global initiative launched in which year?
options: 2020 exactly, matching its name

stem: VISION 2020 aims to eliminate avoidable blindness through which THREE core strategies?
options: Disease control, human resource development, and infrastructure/technology development
Taxation reform, immigration policy, and trade agreements
Military intervention, border security, and customs enforcement
Currency devaluation, interest rate control, and stock market regulation

stem: The SAFE strategy for trachoma control stands for Surgery, Antibiotics, Facial cleanliness, and which other component?
options: Environmental improvement
Emergency evacuation
Economic empowerment
Educational examination only, with no environmental component

stem: In the SAFE strategy for trachoma, the 'S' specifically refers to surgery for which complication?
options: Trichiasis
Cataract
Retinal detachment
Pterygium

stem: Community-Directed Treatment with Ivermectin (CDTI) is specifically used to control which eye disease in endemic Nigerian communities?
options: Onchocerciasis
Trachoma
Cataract
Diabetic retinopathy

stem: Which of the following is explicitly listed as part of the nurse's role in the PREVENTION of blindness?
options: Conducting basic visual acuity screening and recognising danger signs requiring urgent referral
Performing definitive cataract surgery independently without any referral
Prescribing systemic chemotherapy for ocular tumours without specialist input
Issuing final legal disability certifications without any multidisciplinary input

stem: Besides visual acuity screening, which other activity is listed as part of the nurse's role in prevention of blindness, related to newborns?
options: Administering prophylactic eye care to newborns
Performing corneal transplantation on newborns
Prescribing long-term systemic steroids to all newborns
Discharging newborns without any eye assessment whatsoever

stem: The nurse's role in prevention of blindness includes participating in which public health activities?
options: Mass drug administration (ivermectin) and immunisation campaigns
Setting national pharmaceutical pricing policy
Conducting independent clinical drug trials without ethical oversight
Managing the hospital's financial investment portfolio

stem: What is the PRIMARY purpose of health education for blind persons, according to the stated goals?
options: To help the individual understand and accept their condition, and to prepare for rehabilitation and reintegration
To permanently discourage the individual from seeking any further medical care
To isolate the individual from family and community as a protective measure
To replace all medical follow-up with health education alone

stem: A goal of health education for the blind is to prevent further deterioration of remaining vision and prevent complications in which structure, where relevant?
options: The fellow/remaining eye
The unrelated contralateral limb
The unrelated auditory system exclusively
The unrelated gastrointestinal tract exclusively

stem: A goal of health education for the blind is to reduce dependency by teaching which skills?
options: Self-care and orientation/mobility skills
Only advanced calculus and higher mathematics
Only competitive sports techniques unrelated to daily living
Only foreign language acquisition unrelated to daily living

stem: A goal of health education for the blind is to correct misconceptions, stigma, and harmful cultural beliefs about blindness within which groups?
options: The family and community
Only unrelated government regulatory bodies
Only international trade organisations
Only the individual's employer, excluding family and community

stem: Within the content areas of health education for the blind, a person blind from glaucoma in one eye specifically needs education on which point?
options: Protecting and monitoring the other (fellow) eye
Discontinuing all follow-up care for the affected eye permanently
Avoiding any further contact with health care providers
Ignoring any new symptoms in the unaffected eye

stem: Which content area of health education for the blind addresses arranging furniture and objects consistently and marking hazards such as steps and hot surfaces?
options: Home and environmental safety
Legal rights and social welfare schemes
Sexuality and reproductive health education
Vocational assessment

stem: Nutrition, as a content area of health education for the blind, is particularly emphasised when which underlying cause contributed to the blindness?
options: Nutritional deficiency, such as vitamin A deficiency
A purely traumatic cause with no nutritional component
A purely congenital cause present since birth
A purely genetic cause with no modifiable component

stem: Which content area of health education for the blind includes the white cane, guide dog, braille materials, and talking devices?
options: Use of assistive devices
Legal rights and welfare schemes
Psychosocial adjustment
Family and caregiver education

stem: Psychosocial adjustment, as a content area of health education for the blind, involves coping with which experiences?
options: Grief/loss of vision, depression, anxiety, and social withdrawal
Only unrelated financial budgeting concerns
Only unrelated travel logistics
Only unrelated academic examination scheduling

stem: Family and caregiver education, as a content area for the blind, includes addressing which harmful belief that fuels stigma?
options: That blindness is a curse or punishment
That blindness can be fully corrected with simple reading glasses in every case
That blindness always resolves spontaneously within one year
That blindness is a normal and universal part of ageing requiring no support

stem: Which principle of teaching a blind person emphasises that visual demonstration is not possible, so instructions should instead be given how?
options: Through detailed, step-by-step verbal explanation
Through silent written instructions only, with no verbal component
Through brief, vague gestures with no further explanation
Through exclusively visual diagrams with no verbal component

stem: The 'hand-under-hand' technique, used in teaching a blind person, is an example of which teaching method?
options: A touch (tactile) method, guiding the person's hands to feel objects, equipment, or layouts
A purely visual demonstration method
A purely auditory method using only recorded lectures
A purely olfactory method using only scent cues

stem: When teaching a blind person, what should the nurse always do before touching the person or their environment?
options: Announce their presence and identify themselves, and explain what they are about to do
Begin the task immediately without any verbal announcement
Wait for the patient to initiate all physical contact first in every instance
Avoid any verbal communication throughout the entire session

stem: Teaching skills to a blind person in their own real environment, wherever possible, serves which purpose?
options: So that skills learned are directly applicable
So that the nurse can avoid any documentation of the teaching session
So that family members are excluded from the process entirely
So that the session can be shortened to less than one minute

stem: Rehabilitation of the blind is best defined as the process of helping the individual regain maximum possible independence in which domains?
options: Physical, psychological, social, educational, and economic domains
Only financial domains, with no reference to physical or social function
Only religious domains, with no reference to physical or social function
Only recreational domains, with no reference to physical or social function

stem: Which of the following is explicitly listed as a GOAL of rehabilitation of the blind?
options: Restoring the individual's confidence and self-esteem
Ensuring permanent social isolation from family and community
Eliminating the need for any further medical follow-up whatsoever
Guaranteeing complete restoration of normal vision in every case

stem: Medical rehabilitation of the blind includes treatment of the underlying cause where still possible. Which example is given of this?
options: Cataract surgery even after prolonged blindness, which may restore some vision
Amputation of an unrelated limb with no connection to visual function
Tonsillectomy performed regardless of any ocular indication
Appendectomy performed regardless of any ocular indication

stem: Orientation and Mobility (O&M) training, a component of functional/physical rehabilitation, teaches the blind person to move about safely using which specific technique, among others?
options: The long white cane technique
Unassisted running in unfamiliar, obstacle-filled terrain
Riding a bicycle at high speed in dense urban traffic
Climbing unsecured ladders without any orientation training

stem: Besides the white cane and guide dogs, which other orientation and mobility technique involves a family member or companion guiding the blind person correctly?
options: The sighted guide technique
The echo-location technique exclusively, with no human guide involved
The hand-under-hand technique, as used only in teaching, never in mobility
A technique that does not exist in the described rehabilitation framework

stem: Educational rehabilitation of the blind includes teaching reading and writing through which specific medium?
options: Braille
Standard printed text with no adaptation
Sign language exclusively, with no tactile or auditory component
Lip-reading exclusively

stem: Vocational rehabilitation of the blind begins with which activity, to identify suitable trades or occupations?
options: Vocational assessment
Immediate, unassessed job placement with no prior evaluation
Permanent exclusion from the workforce by default
Mandatory retirement regardless of age or ability

stem: Social/psychological rehabilitation of the blind includes support groups and peer counselling, in which blind persons who have successfully adjusted do what?
options: Mentor newly blind individuals
Are excluded from any further contact with newly blind individuals
Are discouraged from discussing their own experience of blindness
Are assigned exclusively administrative, non-supportive roles

stem: What is Community-Based Rehabilitation (CBR)?
options: A strategy that uses community resources to deliver rehabilitation services closer to home, rather than relying solely on centralised institutions
A strategy that relies exclusively on centralised, specialist institutions with no community involvement
A strategy limited strictly to urban tertiary hospitals
A strategy that excludes family members from any involvement in care

stem: Community-Based Rehabilitation (CBR) is described as cost-effective and sustainable, especially given which limitation in Nigeria?
options: A limited number of specialist rehabilitation centres relative to the population in need
An oversupply of specialist rehabilitation centres with excess capacity
A complete absence of any blind population requiring rehabilitation
Unlimited government funding for centralised institutions

stem: CASE SCENARIO: A primary health care nurse in a rural community organizes a 'face-washing' campaign, promotes clean water access, and refers a child with trichiasis for surgical correction, while also recognizing that this same community lies along a fast-flowing river with ongoing blackfly exposure. Which combination of prevention levels and conditions is she addressing?
options: Primary prevention of trachoma through hygiene and water access, and secondary/tertiary intervention for existing trichiasis, while the riverine location also raises her index of suspicion for onchocerciasis
Only tertiary prevention, since all her activities involve surgical referral exclusively
Only primary prevention, since trichiasis referral has no bearing on any level of prevention
An approach irrelevant to Nigerian primary eye care, since trachoma and onchocerciasis never coexist in the same community

stem: CASE SCENARIO: A 68-year-old man presents to a PHC facility with gradual, painless bilateral visual decline over two years, and is found to have elevated intraocular pressure with early optic nerve changes on examination, in a community where cataract surgical backlog is high due to cost and distance. Which combination of diagnosis and health-system factors BEST fits this presentation?
options: His findings are consistent with glaucoma, the 'silent thief of sight,' which can coexist with the separately leading cause of blindness, cataract, whose backlog in this community is driven by poor awareness, cost, distance, and fear of surgery
His findings exclude any possibility of glaucoma, since glaucoma always presents with sudden, severe pain
Cataract and glaucoma can never occur in the same community, so only one diagnosis is possible
His presentation requires no further action, since gradual visual decline after age 60 is always a normal, non-pathological finding

stem: CASE SCENARIO: A nurse is teaching a newly blind adult patient, blind from untreated glaucoma in one eye with early changes now detected in the fellow eye, how to navigate his home safely and use a white cane, while also referring him for vocational assessment. Which combination of rehabilitation and health education principles BEST reflects appropriate care?
options: Health education should emphasize protecting and monitoring the fellow eye, orientation and mobility training should include the long white cane technique, and vocational rehabilitation should begin with an assessment to identify suitable trades
The fellow eye requires no monitoring, since the patient is already blind in one eye
White cane training is unnecessary once a patient has been referred for vocational assessment
Vocational assessment should be skipped entirely in favor of immediate, unassessed job placement

stem: CASE SCENARIO: A community health extension worker (CHEW) identifies a child with a white pupillary reflex during a routine vision screening at a rural school. Which immediate action and underlying concern BEST reflect appropriate recognition of this 'red flag' finding?
options: Urgent referral to a secondary/tertiary eye facility, given that leukocoria (white pupillary reflex) is classically associated with retinoblastoma, a tumour requiring prompt specialist evaluation
Reassurance and discharge with no further action, since a white pupillary reflex in a child is always a normal variant
A recommendation for corrective spectacles alone, since white pupillary reflex is always due to simple refractive error
A diagnosis of trachoma, since trichiasis is the only condition associated with abnormal pupil appearance

stem: CASE SCENARIO: A blind woman and her family attend a community-based rehabilitation (CBR) program where she receives counselling for grief and social withdrawal, her family is educated to avoid both overprotection and neglect, and local community health workers coordinate her care instead of referring her to a distant centralised institution. Which rehabilitation approach and its rationale BEST fit this scenario?
options: Community-Based Rehabilitation, which uses community resources to deliver services closer to home and is considered cost-effective and sustainable given Nigeria's limited number of specialist rehabilitation centres relative to population need
Exclusively medical rehabilitation, since counselling and family education are not recognised components of any rehabilitation framework
An inappropriate approach, since all rehabilitation should occur only in centralised, specialist institutions regardless of distance or cost
Vocational rehabilitation exclusively, since family education and counselling are unrelated to any form of rehabilitation
